title: Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability
desc: Requires deficient care, causation and substantiated loss, distinguishing corrective-fee theories from ethical discipline and adverse outcomes.

kps.k: Malpractice turns on objectively deficient care and causally connected loss, not merely an error, adverse result or honest intention.
kps.d: These decisions distinguish breach, causation and damages as separate requirements. In Cosgrove, the Texas Supreme Court rejects subjective good faith as a defense and evaluates conduct against a reasonably prudent attorney using information available at the time. In Cox-Ott, the Georgia Supreme Court overrules precedent only insofar as it omitted reasonable-care analysis: professional judgment retains protection when lawyers exercise it reasonably. Katsoris likewise protects choices among reasonable alternatives. The practical distinction is between a decision that proved mistaken and a decision reached without adequate care.

qs.q: There is no subjective good faith excuse for attorney negligence.
qs.a: Cosgrove v. Grimes, 774 S.W.2d 662 (Tex. 1989) · Regulators & courts · 1989

qs.q: The jury must evaluate his conduct based on the information the attorney has at the time of the alleged act of negligence.
qs.a: Cosgrove v. Grimes, 774 S.W.2d 662 (Tex. 1989) · Regulators & courts · 1989

kps.k: The claimed injury determines the causation inquiry; corrective fees raise a contested alternative to proving a lost underlying case.
kps.d: Bozelko applies a case-within-a-case inquiry to conviction-related damages. By contrast, the Eighth Circuit's Gerber majority treats fees spent trying to repair privilege waiver as an injury independent of the underlying lawsuit's outcome. Drawing on general causation principles, the Restatement and predominantly supportive decisions elsewhere, it rejects a universal requirement to prove a better litigation outcome. It still requires proof that negligence proximately caused the extra fees and that Gerber would not otherwise have incurred them. The court reversed summary judgment; it did not award damages. These different injury theories should not be treated as a direct conflict between Bozelko and Gerber.

qs.q: More specifically, the plaintiff must prove that, in the absence of the alleged breach of duty by her attorney, "the plaintiff would have prevailed [in] the underlying cause of action and would have been entitled to judgment." _Haddy_ v.
qs.a: Bozelko v. Papastavros, 323 Conn. 275, 147 A.3d 1023 (2016) · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: It makes sense that proving a case-within-a-case is not a hard-and-fast requirement because an attorney’s negligence can result in injuries other than a loss in court.
qs.a: Gerber Products Co. v. Mitchell Williams Selig Gates & Woodyard, PLLC, 28 F.4th 870 (8th Cir. 2022) · Regulators & courts · 2022

kps.k: Gerber leaves the corrective-fee question without a definitive Arkansas Supreme Court answer.
kps.d: The Eighth Circuit predicted Arkansas law rather than applying an existing state supreme court holding on corrective fees. Judge Erickson disputed that prediction and urged certification, stressing the absence of demonstrated disclosure harm apart from an expensive, unsuccessful clawback effort. He conditionally accepted the majority's analysis if Arkansas's highest court recognized such damages. In 2023, the Arkansas Supreme Court rescinded its acceptance of the subsequently certified question without deciding the merits. The state dissent favored answering the question, not a particular substantive answer. The procedural history therefore supplies neither state-court endorsement nor rejection of the federal approach.

qs.q: I am not convinced that the Arkansas Supreme Court would either be (1) persuaded to follow the lead of these states, or (2) would be inclined to adopt the views of § 53 of the Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers.
qs.a: Gerber Products Co. v. Mitchell Williams Selig Gates & Woodyard, PLLC, 28 F.4th 870 (8th Cir. 2022) · Regulators & courts · 2022

qs.q: As explained below, we determine that certification was improvidently granted and rescind  our decision to answer the certified question.
qs.a: Gerber Products Co. v. Mitchell, Williams, Selig, Gates & Woodyard, PLLC, 2023 Ark. 21 · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Plaintiffs must substantiate causation and damages; obvious neglect or general allegations of extra fees do not suffice.
kps.d: Bozelko generally requires expert testimony on causation, subject to obvious-case exceptions, because reconstructing a competent defense's likely outcome exceeds ordinary juror knowledge. The court affirmed judgment against the plaintiff for lacking that evidence, independently of whether breach itself required an expert. It uses an objective reasonable-fact-finder counterfactual, not the original jurors' retrospective preferences. At the pleading stage, Katsoris dismissed unsupported allegations of additional fees and a compelled divorce settlement. Settlement does not itself bar malpractice, but plaintiffs must supply facts supporting ascertainable loss and the required causal connection.

qs.q: [13](http://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4257872/bozelko-v-papastavros/#fn%20%20%20%20%2013) Because a determination of what result should have occurred if the attorney had not been negligent usually is beyond the field of ordinary knowledge and experience possessed by a juror, expert testimony generally will be necessary to provide the essential nexus between the attorney's error and the plaintiff's damages.
qs.a: Bozelko v. Papastavros, 323 Conn. 275, 147 A.3d 1023 (2016) · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: Ethical discipline and alternative claim labels do not substitute for the requirements of civil malpractice.
kps.d: In Hizey, the Washington Supreme Court rejects ethical-code violations both as an independent malpractice cause of action and as evidence of malpractice, opposing the plaintiffs' and some commentators' proposed analogy to statutory violations. It distinguishes discipline's public-protection purpose, which does not require client damage, from negligence liability under Washington's statewide reasonable-lawyer standard. This is a jurisdiction-specific holding, not a universal rule about ethical evidence. Separately, Bozelko requires proximate causation for fiduciary-duty damages, while Katsoris dismisses a fiduciary-duty claim based on the same facts and lacking distinct damages.

qs.q: Because the CPR and RPC explicitly, and in what we deem to be clear and unambiguous language, disclaim any intent to create civil liability standards, we refuse to hold their violation creates a cause of action for malpractice.
qs.a: Hizey v. Carpenter, 119 Wn.2d 251, 830 P.2d 646 (1992) · Regulators & courts · 1992

qs.q: [↵](http://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4257872/bozelko-v-papastavros/) Similarly, a plaintiff alleging a breach of fiduciary duty must show that any damages sustained were proximately caused by the fiduciary's breach of his or her fiduciary duty.
qs.a: Bozelko v. Papastavros, 323 Conn. 275, 147 A.3d 1023 (2016) · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: Recognizing a potentially recoverable injury does not remove evidentiary or timing barriers.
kps.d: The practical implication is to identify the particular loss, connect it to a specific breach, support any specialized counterfactual with expert evidence, and address the applicable limitations rule. In federal Gerber, Arkansas's three-year period ran from negligence rather than discovery, absent concealment. Further proceedings depended on proving timely negligence in the February 2016 document production and its causal connection to the injury. The earlier privilege decision did not itself establish that negligence. The supplied decisions concern conventional representation failures; they do not establish an AI-specific standard of care or liability rule.

vlens.an:
The selected judicial sources support the proposition that attorney error, an adverse result, ethical misconduct, or honest intention does not alone establish civil malpractice. Their common reasoning separates objectively deficient care from causation and substantiated damages: Cosgrove and Cox-Ott apply reasonable-care standards rather than subjective good faith; Katsoris requires actual, ascertainable loss and protects choices among reasonable alternatives; Bozelko requires a supported causal counterfactual, generally through expert testimony where the issue exceeds ordinary juror knowledge; and Hizey keeps professional discipline distinct from civil liability.

Material variation concerns how those requirements apply, not whether they exist. Bozelko uses a case-within-a-case analysis for conviction-related loss, whereas the Eighth Circuit’s Gerber majority treats corrective fees as a potentially independent injury while still requiring negligence and a complete causal chain. That corrective-fee approach remains a federal prediction of Arkansas law: the Arkansas Supreme Court rescinded certification without resolving it, and the federal dissent questioned the prediction. Hizey’s exclusion of ethical-rule violations as malpractice evidence is also expressly jurisdiction-specific, while Gerber adds separate limitations and evidentiary barriers. Thus, these curated authorities support the proposition’s core while differing over particular injury theories, proof requirements, and jurisdictional doctrine; their number should not be read as evidence of prevalence among courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: The plaintiff must prove that there is a duty owed to him by the defendant, a breach of that duly, that the breach proximately caused the plaintiff injury and that damages occurred.
qs.a: Cosgrove v. Grimes, 774 S.W.2d 662 (Tex. 1989) · Regulators & courts · 1989

qs.q: If Gerber can also demonstrate that it “would not have incurred the fees in the absence of the [firm’s] negligence,” it will have completed the necessary causal chain.
qs.a: Gerber Products Co. v. Mitchell Williams Selig Gates & Woodyard, PLLC, 28 F.4th 870 (8th Cir. 2022) · Regulators & courts · 2022

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources support the cluster’s principal proposition by establishing that legal malpractice requires more than an error, adverse outcome, or improper conduct in the abstract. Both decisions require an objective breach of professional care together with causation and actual client loss. Cosgrove supplies the core negligence principle: an attorney’s subjective good faith does not excuse care falling below the reasonably prudent attorney standard, assessed using the information available at the relevant time. Hizey reaches the same overall position while addressing a different boundary, separating professional discipline from civil liability and requiring duty, breach, damage, and proximate causation rather than treating an ethical-rule violation as malpractice by itself. The material internal variation concerns emphasis, not direction: Cosgrove focuses on objective care versus honest intention, whereas Hizey focuses on the separate functions of ethical regulation and malpractice law and adopts the jurisdiction-specific position that ethical violations are not even evidence of malpractice. These curated cases do not address the synthesis’s later disputes over corrective fees, case-within-a-case proof, expert evidence, or limitations, but they provide its foundational liability framework.

qs.q: There is no subjective good faith excuse for attorney negligence.
qs.a: Cosgrove v. Grimes, 774 S.W.2d 662 (Tex. 1989) · Regulators & courts · 1989

elens.an: The selected 2015–2022 decisions support the proposition that attorney error alone does not establish malpractice. Bozelko and Katsoris treat deficient care, causation, and actual loss as distinct requirements: Bozelko requires a substantiated causal link—generally supported by expert testimony where the counterfactual outcome is specialized—while Katsoris rejects both reasonable strategic choices as malpractice and conclusory assertions of additional fees or financial harm as ascertainable damages. Gerber materially varies the application rather than rejecting the core rule: its majority predicts that corrective fees may constitute an injury independent of losing the underlying case, so a case-within-a-case is not invariably required, but recovery still depends on proving negligence and a causal connection to those fees. Its separate opinion questions that state-law prediction and favors certification, underscoring that the corrective-fee theory was unsettled rather than definitively established under Arkansas law. These curated sources therefore converge on the need for proven breach, causation, and substantiated injury while differing over what injury can qualify and how causation must be shown.

qs.q: It makes sense that proving a case-within-a-case is not a hard-and-fast requirement because an attorney’s negligence can result in injuries other than a loss in court.
qs.a: Gerber Products Co. v. Mitchell Williams Selig Gates & Woodyard, PLLC, 28 F.4th 870 (8th Cir. 2022) · Regulators & courts · 2022

elens.an: The 2023 source supports the proposition that malpractice liability requires more than an alleged error or expense: even under the corrective-fee theory, Gerber still had to prove that the firm’s negligence caused fees it otherwise would not have incurred. It also reinforces the synthesis’s narrower proposition that the claimed injury shapes the causation inquiry, because corrective fees were treated by the Eighth Circuit as potentially independent of whether Gerber would have obtained a better result in the underlying litigation. Material internal variation concerns whether Arkansas law recognizes that injury theory at all. The district court required proof of a better underlying outcome, the Eighth Circuit rejected that as universally necessary, and Judge Erickson characterized the federal majority’s approach as an uncharted expansion. The Arkansas Supreme Court ultimately rescinded certification without resolving the merits, while its dissent favored answering the question but did not endorse either substantive answer. Thus, the source supports the cluster’s causation-and-loss framework and its account of unresolved Arkansas law, without establishing that corrective fees are recoverable in Arkansas.

elens.an: The 2025 source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Cox-Ott holds that legal malpractice turns on whether the lawyer exercised reasonable care, not simply whether professional judgment later proved mistaken or produced an adverse outcome. It also treats breach and but-for causation as distinct requirements, reinforcing the synthesis’s insistence on deficient care plus causally connected loss. Its principal refinement is that protection for professional judgment survives, but only where the judgment was reached with reasonable care; honest intention alone is insufficient. The source does not materially address damages substantiation, corrective-fee theories, ethical discipline, limitations, or AI-specific standards, so its support is strongest for the proposition’s core breach-and-causation framework rather than every aspect of the broader synthesis. Because the supplied 2025 evidence consists of one decision, it establishes that decision’s relationship to the proposition and should not be treated as representative of all courts or sources in the period.

qs.q: Rather, attorneys enjoy discretion in matters of professional judgment, and the inquiry focuses on whether the attorney used reasonable care in exercising that judgment which later proved to be mistaken.
qs.a: Cox-Ott v. Barnes & Thornburg, LLP, 321 Ga. 688, 915 S.E.2d 894 (2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025
